_comment: Adventures (docs/ADVENTURES.md §5.2, §6, §8.5; game/story/forge.py): blueprints, each forged into an adventure when its hook is taken. max_active: how many a hero carries at once. words: nested tables for the story's text. epithets: what the epilogue offers, by tag.

dusk: the light going amber over the hills
the last of the day leaving the fields
the long shadows reaching for the road
carcass: what is left of a big ox, opened along the belly
the remains of a carter's mule, half of it gone
a cow, or what was a cow, dragged a long way from its field
track: marks in the soft earth as broad as a shield, pressed deep
a furrow where something heavy dragged its kill
the bark of an old ash torn away higher than a man can reach
beast_witness: "I was on the hill road with the cart," {witness} says, and has to stop. "It came out of the scrub like the ground itself was getting up. It took the ox, not me. It looked at me, and took the ox."
{witness} will not look at you while they tell it. "Big as a haywain. It went up towards {home} with half the carcass in its jaws, and I never heard it breathe hard once."
"They'll tell you I was drunk," says {witness}. "I wasn't. It stopped in the road to look at me. Then it went back towards {home}, slow, like it had all the time there is."
{witness} shows you the scar first. "It did that going past, without even stopping. If it had stopped I'd be dead. It wasn't hungry for me. Not that night."
witness_tale: {witness} tells you what they saw, and their hands shake the whole time.
"I saw it," {witness} says. "I wish to every god I hadn't."
{witness} tells it plainly, as if they had told it many times to themselves in the dark.
patron_brief: "{goal}" {patron} says. "That is all I know to tell you. Go carefully."
{patron} counts it off on their fingers. "{goal} After that, you know more than I do."

beast.name: The Beast of {place}
title: The Beast of {town}
The Hunt for {villain}
{villain_short} of {home}
What Walks Above {town}
The Hunger at {town}
hook: {patron} meets you at the door with the look of someone who has not slept. "It is {villain}. It has come down from {home} again, and this time it took one of ours. You have the look of someone who could finish it."
"We have sent to the lord, and the lord sent no one," says {patron}. "{villain} has killed at {town} and it will kill again. Whatever we can pay is yours, if you will hunt it."
The whole of {town} seems to be at the well when you come, and the talk is all of {villain}. It is {patron} who asks you plainly: will you go up to {home} and put an end to it?
{patron} has the hide of a dog that was torn in half laid out on the table. "That was the bravest dog in {town}," they say. "{villain} did that in the dark, in a breath. Will you hunt it?"
premise: A named killer of the old songs has come down from {home} on {town}: find what it is, learn what it fears, and kill it in its den.
{villain} is killing round {town} again. Read its kills, find the one who saw it, learn what it fears, and finish it at {home}.
{town} is being eaten, a family at a time, by {villain} out of {home}. Somebody has to learn how it can be killed, and then go up and do it.

title: The Killings
Blood on the Hill Road
What Came Down in the Night
goal: Go to where it last killed, read what it left, and find who saw it.
opening: {town} counts its dead. Somewhere on the road below {home} is the last of them, and the one who lived.
The first thing is to see what it did. The second is to find the one who saw it do it.
Every hunt begins with the kill. {villain_short} left one on the road out of {town}, not two days ago.
reveal: There is no doubt now. This is {villain}, that took {victim} in {victim_year} and has been fed on the fear of {area} ever since. It sleeps at {home}, and it is not afraid of anything that has hunted it yet.
The old ones of {town} know the name, once they are made to say it: {villain}. It killed {victim}, years ago, and came back for more. Its den is {home}.
Tracks, a name and a den: {villain}, the {beast} of the old songs, that killed {victim} in {victim_year}. Nobody has gone up to {home} after it and come back whole.

title: The Hunt's Price
What It Fears
Bait or Blood
goal: Learn what will hurt it, get the means, and choose how to bring it to you.
opening: Nobody kills {villain} by walking up to it. You need to know what it fears, and to carry it with you.
{patron} has done their part: they have told you everything they know. The rest is yours to find out.
A beast that has lived through every hunt has a weakness, or it would have died. Find it.
reveal: It came, and it bled, and it ran. Now it is in {home} with its wound, and there is nowhere else for it to go. Neither is there for you.
{villain_short} knows you now. It will be waiting in the dark of {home}, and it will not run again.
You have hurt it, and it has gone back to its den to lick the wound. It is now or never: up to {home}.

title: The Den
Into {home}
The Last of {villain_short}
goal: Go up to {home} and finish it.
opening: The way to {home} is short, and seems long. You will not need to look for {villain_short}: it knows you are coming.
{town} watches you go. Some of them pray; the rest only stand at the edge of the fields and wait.
There is nothing left to learn and nothing left to buy. There is only {home}, and what sleeps in it.

warning: The air beyond this point stinks of old blood and rot. Whatever lives here is very close, and it is awake.
Bones underfoot, gnawed white, and a breathing in the dark ahead that is not yours.
This is the end of the den. Rest now if you mean to, because there will be no rest beyond it.
first: It rises from the bones, and keeps rising.
It knows you. It has been waiting.
Its eyes take the torchlight and give back none of it.

place: {town} sleeps with its doors unbarred for the first time in a year. The children are let out to the fields again, though their mothers still count them at dusk.
The people of {town} dragged what was left of {villain_short} into the square and burned it there. Everyone came to watch, and nobody cheered until it was ash.
There is a new song in the inn at {town}, and it is about you. It is not a good song, but they sing it every night.
{town} hung the skull of {villain} over the door of its hall, and the elders swear the flocks are fatter for it already.
patron: {patron} paid what they promised, and would have paid twice. "I did not think anyone would come," they said. "Nobody ever does."
{patron} keeps a seat by the fire for you, they say, should you ever come back to {town}.
{patron} has sent word to every farm in {area}: whoever shelters you, shelters a friend of {town}.
{patron} went out afterwards, alone, to see the body for themselves. They came back and said nothing at all for a day.
ally: {ally} has the beast's old runs for a trap-line now, and says the hares are bolder than they were.
{ally} tells the tale in the inn whenever someone buys the ale, and makes your part bigger every time.
{ally} went back to the woods. They say they think of you when the light goes.
{ally} is the one the villages call for now, when something is at the flocks.
witness: {witness} still will not take the hill road. But they sleep, now.
{witness} came to see the body, to be sure. They stood over it a long time.
{witness} lit a candle at the shrine for the ones who did not come back, and one for you.
{witness} has told it so often that they half believe they were brave.
hero: You came back to {town} with blood to the elbow and the name {villain} in every mouth.
The hunt is over. You are a little more than you were: someone who hunted {villain} and lived.
Somewhere a minstrel is already getting it wrong. That is what it is to be remembered.
You will not forget {villain}. Neither, now, will anyone in {area}.

place: {town} is empty. The doors hang open and the hearths are cold. {villain} has the fields.
The last cart left {town} with the dawn. Whoever stays now stays with {villain}.
Nobody tends the graves at {town} now. The grass is up to the windows.
{town} stands, but nobody lives in it. They say the beast walks the street at night.
patron: {patron} went with the others, and did not look back at you.
{patron} is somewhere on the roads with what is left of {town}.
{patron} asked you to hunt it. You did not, in time. They will not ask anyone again.
Nobody knows where {patron} went when {town} emptied.
hero: It won. Not every hunt ends with a body.
{villain} still lives at {home}, fatter than it was.
There will be other hunters. Perhaps they will be in time.
You will hear the name {villain} again. It will not be a kind story.

place: {town} waits for someone else to come.
In {town} they still speak of the hunter who came and went.
{town} bars its doors at dusk, as it did before you came.
{villain} is not dead. {town} knows it every night.
hero: You left the hunt to others.
Some tales are not yours to finish.
The road took you elsewhere, and {home} is behind you.
